title: API 510 Training in Denver: Online Pressure Vessel Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Denver vessel inspectors: Commerce City refinery vessels, Weld County gas plants and Colorado's owner-user law. Instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Denver: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Refinery, Gas Plant and Contract Inspectors on the Front Range
html:
API 510 exam prep for vessel inspectors along the Front Range

Colorado has a single refinery, Suncor's plant in Commerce City about six miles from downtown Denver, and much of the pressure vessel work around the city happens elsewhere: at gas processing plants in Weld County, at contract inspection companies covering sites from the Front Range into Wyoming, and in shops that build or repair vessels. That matters for exam preparation, because the pressure vessel inspector examination is written around refinery and chemical plant vessels while many local working hours go on equipment it treats differently.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Denver. You study the API 510 course online, at your own pace, and send questions to an instructor whenever a clause or a calculation stops you. The American Petroleum Institute sets the eligibility rules, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and certifies the candidates who pass; the course prepares you for that day and nothing more.

Commerce City: one refinery assembled from three plants

Suncor's own history of the site explains a lot about the vessels you would inspect there. Plant 1 broke ground in 1931 in what was then Commerce Town, a separate refinery known as Plant 2 followed in 1937, and Plant 3 was added in the 1970s to process heavier crude from Montana. Suncor bought Plants 1 and 3 from ConocoPhillips in 2003 and Plant 2 from Valero in 2005, and now runs them together. The company describes the result as a refinery of approximately 103,000 barrels a day, operating around the clock, buying crude from the Denver-Julesburg Basin and selling nearly 95% of its products inside Colorado.

EIA's refinery capacity survey, which reports capacity at the start of 2026, still lists two entries, Commerce City East and Commerce City West, at 36,000 and 67,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation. The rest of its figures, in barrels per stream day, sketch the vessel population:

  • Crude and vacuum distillation. Vacuum units of 8,500 (east) and 25,000 (west) behind the crude towers, so desalters, atmospheric and vacuum columns, overhead accumulators and a long train of exchanger shells. On the exam these raise hydrochloric acid corrosion in overhead systems and sulfidation in the hot sections, both on the current RP 571 list.
  • Fluid catalytic cracking. Fresh feed capacity of 9,000 at the east plant and 21,000 at the west, which means reactors, regenerators, main fractionators and the drums of the gas concentration section, where erosion and wet H2S damage are the mechanisms to know.
  • Hydrotreating and reforming. Low-pressure catalytic reformers of 11,000 and 10,900, naphtha hydrotreating at both plants, and kerosene and jet, diesel and heavy gas oil hydrotreating at the west plant. Reactors and high-pressure separators in hydrogen service bring high-temperature hydrogen attack and high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion into the picture.
  • Sulfur, hydrogen and asphalt. Because this is Colorado's sole refinery, EIA's state production capacity totals are effectively the plant's: 116 short tons a day of sulfur, 22 million cubic feet a day of hydrogen and 13,200 barrels a day of asphalt and road oil. Sulfur recovery comes with amine contactors, regenerators and sour water strippers, which is where amine stress corrosion cracking and wet H2S damage live.

EIA lists no coking at either plant, so coke drums are not part of the Commerce City picture. The list is a guide to the job, not to the exam. The examination takes damage mechanism questions only from the RP 571 sections named in its Body of Knowledge, and the course teaches to that list.

Colorado's boiler law names API-certified inspectors

Colorado's boiler and pressure vessel statute, Title 9, Article 4, administered by the Division of Oil and Public Safety, writes the API route into its definitions. Section 9-4-101 defines an owner-user inspection organization as an owner or user of pressure-retaining items with a regularly established inspection department whose organization and procedures meet the National Board's rules or the American Petroleum Institute's API 510 program and are acceptable to the director. An owner-user inspector, in the same section, is either a holder of a National Board owner-user commission who has passed the National Board's examination or an API-certified inspector working under a jurisdictionally approved owner-user inspection organization.

Section 9-4-110.5 then sets out what an approved organization must do. It inspects its nonexempt boilers and pressure vessels using qualified personnel, keeps a signed copy of each report where the equipment is, tells the director promptly about anything unsafe, keeps records listing each unit with its last and next inspection dates and its repairs, and sends the director an annual statement signed by the person supervising the inspections. A state-issued certificate of inspection is still required for equipment inspected this way, and inspectors must carry liability insurance suited to the work.

The Division's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Regulations, 7 CCR 1101-5, add detail. In the revision the Division filed in 2017 they incorporate API 510 for in-service inspection, repair, alteration and rerating of pressure vessels in the petroleum and chemical processing industries, alongside the National Board Inspection Code for boilers and other pressure-retaining items, and they name a specific edition of each. That edition is not necessarily the one you will be examined on. API's Body of Knowledge says plainly that some jurisdictions work to editions other than those on the effectivity sheet and that the exam follows the effectivity sheet, so learn the current edition for the exam and your state's adopted edition for the job.

Gas plant vessels in Weld County, and the part of API 510 the exam leaves out

North of Denver the DJ Basin keeps a different set of vessels busy. Chevron runs its Colorado oil and gas business from a regional headquarters in Denver and concentrates on the liquids-rich part of Weld County; Oxy says it has operated in the basin for more than 30 years; and SM Energy, based in Denver, completed its all-stock merger with Civitas Resources early in 2026. Production from those leases is gathered to processing plants. Western Midstream, for example, lists five active gas processing plants in its DJ Basin complex, at Platte Valley, Fort Lupton, Wattenberg, Lancaster and Latham, the last two with two trains each, plus a central oil stabilization facility for high-vapor-pressure crude from the Wattenberg field.

A gas plant is full of pressure vessels, from inlet separators and amine contactors to dehydrators, stabilizers and the cold sections that recover natural gas liquids, and API 510 has long treated much of the upstream world differently. The 2006 edition, which is publicly available through the federal incorporation-by-reference library, says vessels in exploration and production service, such as drilling, producing, gathering, lease processing and treating, may be inspected under alternative rules in a separate section, and it leaves each owner free to choose suitable inspection and recording systems within the limits of its jurisdiction.

What matters for the exam is that the Body of Knowledge for the September 2026, January 2027 and May 2027 windows lists "rules for natural resource vessels, API 510, Section 9" among the topics candidates are not expected to know, along with cryogenic vessels below minus 50 °F. A Weld County candidate therefore has to learn the refinery and chemical plant rules thoroughly for the examination, even if day-to-day work runs under a production programme. The mechanisms you meet at a gas plant do carry over: amine stress corrosion cracking, wet H2S damage, brittle fracture and corrosion under insulation are all on the examined RP 571 list.

Wyoming refineries within a Denver inspector's reach

Denver-based contract inspectors often travel north for turnarounds. EIA's 2026 survey lists four operating Wyoming refineries with 127,000 barrels per calendar day of crude capacity between them.

SinclairHF Sinclair Wyoming Refining Co75,000Vacuum distillation and a delayed coker of 20,000 barrels per stream day
Evansville, near CasperHF Sinclair Casper Refining Company31,000No vacuum or coking capacity listed

EvanstonSilver Eagle Refining3,000No vacuum or coking capacity listed

Cheyenne is missing from that table for a reason. HF Sinclair ran the last crude through its Cheyenne refinery in August 2020 and says the conversion to a renewable diesel unit was completed in 2021; the unit processes refined soybean oil and animal fats at about 6,000 barrels a day. For a vessel inspector, a site like that is a practical lesson in change of service. The vessels are the same steel, but the fluids, temperatures and corrosion behaviour are not, so the damage mechanism assumptions behind every inspection plan have to be revisited, and any change to a vessel's design temperature, minimum design metal temperature or MAWP is a rerating that API 510's rules govern.

Worked example: static head at the bottom of a tall column

Denver-area vessel work includes plenty of towers, and the Body of Knowledge tells you how the exam handles their liquid: all static head is based on a specific gravity of 1.0, and you should know the conversion factor of 0.433 psi per foot. Here is the sort of question that catches candidates who calculate the top of the vessel and stop.

  1. A column has a maximum allowable working pressure of 50 psi at the top. Its lowest shell course sits 70 ft below the highest liquid level.
  2. Static head at that course: 70 × 0.433 = 30.3 psi. Pressure the course must hold: 50 + 30.3 = 80.3 psi.
  3. Take an inside radius of 48 in. in the corroded condition, an allowable stress of 20,000 psi given in the question and a joint efficiency of 0.85, so SE = 17,000 psi.
  4. Required thickness under UG-27(c)(1): t = PR ÷ (SE − 0.6P) = (80.3 × 48) ÷ (17,000 − 48.2) = 3,854 ÷ 16,952 = 0.227 in.
  5. Had you ignored static head, the same formula would give (50 × 48) ÷ (17,000 − 30) = 0.141 in., an underestimate of almost nine hundredths of an inch.
  6. If that course now measures 0.250 in. and corrodes at 0.004 in. a year, remaining life is (0.250 − 0.227) ÷ 0.004, about 5.7 years, and the internal or on-stream interval is the lesser of half that, about 2.8 years, and 10 years.

Drums and exchanger shells mounted low in a structure need the same treatment.

Routes into API 510 from Denver jobs

Eligibility is a combination of education and inspection experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency; the API 510 certification requirements page sets out the four routes. In practice Denver candidates tend to come from one of these backgrounds.

  • Engineers. Colorado School of Mines in Golden offers a Bachelor of Science in Metallurgical and Materials Engineering that includes welding and joining, backed by its Center for Welding, Joining and Coatings Research. An engineering degree puts you on the one-year experience route, provided that year is spent supervising or performing inspection as the code describes it.
  • Welders and fabricators. Red Rocks Community College offers an AAS in Welding at its Lakewood campus, plus process certificates. Whether a particular welding degree counts as a two-year engineering or technology qualification is API's decision, so describe it accurately on your application; if it does not count, the high school route applies.
  • NDT technicians. Thickness readers and MT, PT and UT technicians who work refinery and gas plant outages already know vessels from the outside in; keep records of the inspection scopes you work. For the NDT side, see NDT training in Denver.
  • Operators. Process operators bring knowledge of how a unit runs, which helps with damage mechanism questions, but qualifying years start when inspection work starts.

Fitting the course around Front Range work

Field days in Weld County or Wyoming can mean long drives and little desk time, so plan by phases rather than by weeks: the API 510 code and its calculations first, then ASME Section VIII with the welding and NDE documents, then timed practice papers, sending questions to the instructor as they come up. Prometric lists test centres in and around Denver, and you book a seat once API accepts your application for a window.

Sponsoring vessel inspectors from a Denver-area employer

An owner-user inspection organization in Colorado needs inspectors who qualify under the statute, and contract inspection firms that serve such organizations face the same expectation. Employers can enrol several candidates at once, each working at a pace that fits their shifts. Fees are quoted on request, and each candidate still applies to API individually, with the employer usually confirming the experience the application describes.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 class I can attend in person in Denver?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Denver, and the API 510 course has no timetable: you enrol, study online at your own pace and send questions to an instructor whenever you need help. When API accepts your application you book the examination itself at a Prometric test centre, and Prometric lists centres in and around Denver.

faq.q: Does Colorado accept API 510 certification for owner-user inspections?
faq.a: Colorado's statute defines an owner-user inspector as either a holder of a National Board owner-user commission who has passed the National Board examination or an API-certified inspector working under a jurisdictionally approved owner-user inspection organization. The organization itself must be approved by the director, and its procedures must meet the National Board's rules or the API 510 program. Certification alone does not make you an owner-user inspector; the approved organization is part of the definition.

faq.q: I inspect separators and amine units at a Weld County gas plant. Is that what the API 510 exam tests?
faq.a: Partly. The current Body of Knowledge excludes the API 510 rules for natural resource vessels, so the exam assumes refinery and chemical plant practice for intervals, corrosion rates and records. The damage mechanisms you see every day are another matter: amine stress corrosion cracking, wet H2S damage and corrosion under insulation are all on the examined RP 571 list, so your plant experience will help with those questions.

faq.q: Does inspection work at the Cheyenne renewable diesel unit count toward API 510 experience?
faq.a: It can, but API decides. What counts is supervising or performing vessel inspection as the code describes it, for or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, within the last 10 years. A renewable diesel unit is still a process plant full of pressure vessels, so describe your duties precisely and let API's verification settle it.

faq.q: I hold a National Board commission as a special inspector for an insurer in Colorado. Do I also need API 510?
faq.a: Not for your insurance work, which the statute ties to the National Board commission. API 510 matters if you move into an owner-user inspection department or a contractor serving one, because the Colorado definition of an owner-user inspector recognises API-certified inspectors under an approved organization. Many inspectors hold both.

faq.q: Are cryogenic NGL vessels covered on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Not as an engineering topic. The Body of Knowledge lists cryogenic vessels below minus 50 °F among the ASME requirements candidates are not expected to know. Brittle fracture is examined, though, through RP 571 and the impact test and minimum design metal temperature rules of Section VIII, so a cold-service background is still useful.

faq.q: Colorado's rule names an older API 510 edition. Which one will I be examined on?
faq.a: The edition on the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your exam window. API's Body of Knowledge notes that some jurisdictions work to editions other than those on the effectivity sheet, and states that the examination is based on the effectivity sheet editions. Learn the current text for the exam, and check your site's procedures and the Division's adopted edition for the job itself.

faq.q: Can a Denver inspection contractor enrol several vessel inspectors together?
faq.a: Yes. A contractor or owner-user department can sponsor a group, each inspector working through the course at a pace that suits their rotation. Fees are quoted on request through the enquiry link on this page, and each inspector still applies to API individually, so plan who is aiming at which window.
